diagnostic.prompt: Before calculating together-time, what should you combine?

choices.text: Add the fractions of the job each person completes in one hour, then take the reciprocal.
choices.feedback: Right. Work rates add because both people contribute during the same hour. The combined rate is jobs per hour; its reciprocal gives hours per job.

choices.text: Add the two completion times.
choices.feedback: Those are the times each person would need alone. To combine simultaneous workers, add the amount of the job each completes per hour.

choices.text: Average the two completion times.
choices.feedback: The mean time does not account for how much work each person contributes in the same hour. Convert each time to a rate first.

choices.text: Use only the faster person’s completion time.
choices.feedback: The faster person works at that rate, but the second person adds more work during each hour. Combine both rates.

choices.text: I am unsure, guessed, or used another approach.
choices.feedback: No cause is established. Ask: what fraction of the job does each person finish in one hour?

diagnostic.confirmation: Was that the reasoning you used before answering, did you choose it after seeing these choices, did you guess, or did you misclick? A selected option is only a hypothesis.

verified_answer.method: reciprocal of the sum of individual unit-work rates

steps: In one hour, the first worker completes 1/3 of the job.
In one hour, the second worker completes 1/6 of the job.
Together they complete 1/3 + 1/6 = 1/2 of the job per hour.
Time = 1 ÷ 1/2 = 2 hours.
hints: A completion time is not the same as a work rate.
Find the fraction of the whole job each person completes in one hour.
Add those hourly fractions, then ask how many hours are needed for one whole job.
worked_solution.shortcut: For two constant-rate workers completing the same job together: time = (first time × second time) ÷ (first time + second time). Check that the result is shorter than either solo time.
